title: Grandmentor

jokes.text: Gassy Patsy walk-on contest callback — robotic voice saying 'keep the white house white'
jokes.setup: Jack brags about the TGS viewer walk-on contest as great promotion, referencing last year
jokes.punchline: The flashback reveals a contestant named 'Gassy Patsy' delivering a racist robotic message to audience boos — the 'promotion' was a disaster
jokes.explanation: The compressed absurdity — a contest entrant named 'Gassy Patsy' speaking in a robotic voice with a racist slogan — is maximally efficient dark comedy. The audience boos function as the punchline punctuation. Strong originality and economy.

jokes.text: 'You know who enters these walk-on contests? Weirdos.' — followed by an essay typed on the inside of a bloody halter top
jokes.setup: Jack defends the contest; Liz says weirdos enter
jokes.punchline: Confirmation: one essay is literally typed on the inside of a bloody halter top
jokes.explanation: Textbook 30 Rock structure: the generic setup ('weirdos enter these contests') is immediately paid off with a hyper-specific, viscerally wrong detail. 'Typed on the inside of a bloody halter top' is excellent economy — every word adds to the wrongness. Earns its score through specificity and structure.

jokes.text: 'I thought you said a man should never wear pastel unless he's a black guy on Easter.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz to pick a tie, implying his usual rules
jokes.punchline: Liz quotes Jack's own absurdly specific fashion rule back at him, revealing how eccentric and specific his worldview is
jokes.explanation: Extremely high character integration — this joke only works because of Jack's established pomposity about masculine codes of dress, AND it's filtered through Liz having absorbed his worldview. The specificity ('black guy on Easter') is the kind of absurdly precise bigotry-adjacent snobbery that defines Jack. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'I need to tone down my natural aura of strength and sexual dominance. Which wasn't going to happen with the tie I was going to wear.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains he's going on The Today Show to talk about Avery
jokes.punchline: His stated problem is managing his overwhelming masculine power for public consumption, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Pure Jack Donaghy character comedy. The deadpan delivery of 'aura of strength and sexual dominance' as a real practical problem is the joke. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: 'Amnesty International is nothing but a company that makes and sells candles. That explains all the vigils. That is a good scam.'
jokes.setup: Jack lists failures in getting Avery freed — UN useless, State Dept full of Democrats
jokes.punchline: Amnesty International revealed as a candle company; Liz's 'that explains all the vigils' is the second punchline landing perfectly
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The absurdist premise (Amnesty International = candle company) is genuinely original, but the double punchline structure is what elevates it to exceptional: Jack's revelation + Liz's 'that explains all the vigils' + Jack's 'it's a good scam.' Three beats that escalate perfectly. Highly quotable, rewatch-worthy, and the logic is airtight within the show's absurdist universe.

jokes.text: 'Media is a plural noun. Put this tie on.'
jokes.setup: Jack says 'the media have moved on' — grammatically correct but unusual
jokes.punchline: Liz ignores the emotional content to correct him on grammar, then pivots to the mundane task without pause
jokes.explanation: Economy score is near-perfect — five words deliver a character beat (Liz as grammar pedant), a joke about misplaced priorities, and a pivot back to action. Pure Liz Lemon. The structure (emotional moment → grammar correction → mundane command) is a classic 30 Rock rhythm executed crisply.

jokes.text: Matt Lauer's band: 'Rhythm and News' — 'It's blues rock, Lemon.'
jokes.setup: Jack says he'll do whatever it takes to get Avery's story back out, including see Matt Lauer's band
jokes.punchline: 'Rhythm and News' — the band name pun plus Jack's disgusted description 'It's blues rock, Lemon' treating this as a genuine sacrifice
jokes.explanation: The pun itself is solid ('Rhythm and Blues' → 'Rhythm and News'), but the real joke is the escalating absurdity of Jack's sacrifice framing — ending on a celebrity's bad band name. The beat pause before the reveal is structurally clean.

jokes.text: Kenneth's confessional: 'I know I'm a big shot now with my suits and a desk lamp that I control'
jokes.setup: Kenneth addresses the camera about his new job at Standards and Practices
jokes.punchline: His markers of success — 'suits' and 'a desk lamp that I control' — are pathetically modest, delivered with genuine pride
jokes.explanation: The desk lamp detail is perfectly Kenneth — his humility is so extreme that a lamp he controls is a status symbol. Very high character integration. The delivery of 'that I control' as a genuine point of pride is the punchline.

jokes.text: The Standards and Practices department is called out by name — its employee, Gaylord Felcher, presents the 'Employee of the F***ing Week' award while bleeping himself
jokes.setup: Kenneth receives a fancy award from his new department
jokes.punchline: The Standards and Practices department — TV's censorship body — is itself profane, with a rep named 'Gaylord Felcher' presenting an award full of bleeps
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly layered meta-joke: Standards & Practices (the real NBC department that bleeps profanity) is depicted as profane itself. 'Gaylord Felcher' as the employee name is a layered joke — a name that itself would be censored in some contexts, presented by the censorship body. The irony is dense and earned. This is exceptional 30 Rock craft — institutional satire + meta-commentary + a gag name all compressed into 15 seconds.

jokes.text: 'What's your problem?' / 'Oh my, well... my parents were technically brothers—' / 'Look, I'm trying to do my job here.'
jokes.setup: Hazel confronts Kenneth and asks what his problem is
jokes.punchline: Kenneth begins to sincerely explain his deeply inbred family background as a literal answer to 'what's your problem'
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection: 'what's your problem' is idiom, but Kenneth takes it literally, beginning to reveal that his parents 'were technically brothers' — an amazing dark detail delivered in Kenneth's signature earnest tone. Hazel cutting him off before he can finish is perfect structure. Highly character-specific.

jokes.text: 'He has a special place in my heart. Just like Nana Parcell, my heartworm.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth says Tracy has a special place in his heart
jokes.punchline: He clarifies with a comparison to his heartworm, named 'Nana Parcell' — implying he has an actual parasitic worm in his heart that he's named after his grandmother
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is a sincere cliché ('special place in my heart'), the punchline reveals Kenneth has a literal heartworm he's named after his grandmother. Every element is doing work: the rural poverty backstory, the warmth Kenneth feels even toward a parasite, the name 'Nana Parcell.' Could only be Kenneth. Exceptional character integration, originality, and economy.

jokes.text: Mine collapse in China — all miners are babies paid in yogurt; puppies lowered to bring supplies
jokes.setup: Jack's segment is bumped for real news — a mine collapse in China
jokes.punchline: The 'real news': all Chinese miners are babies paid in yogurt, and adult dogs can't fit in the mines so puppies are lowered in with supplies
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist escalation. The joke has two beats that compound: (1) baby miners paid in yogurt — already a complete, hilarious absurdist premise, and then (2) the puppies detail, which escalates the cute-animal dimension perfectly. Jack's sighing 'Remember when we used to be the world leader in baby cuteness?' is the cherry on top. One of the episode's strongest pure laugh moments.

jokes.text: 'Remember when we used to be the world leader in baby cuteness? I can't compete with that.'
jokes.setup: Jack just heard that baby miners + puppies bumped his Avery segment
jokes.punchline: Jack frames America's geopolitical decline in terms of 'baby cuteness world leadership' — treating it as a genuine national crisis
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke — Jack's corporate/nationalist worldview applied to baby cuteness as a geopolitical metric. Flows naturally from the baby miners joke and enriches it. Best read as an extension of joke #12.

jokes.text: 'Yes, I didn't expect you to play for four hours.' (re: Matt Lauer's band, after four hours of blues rock)
jokes.setup: Matt Lauer thanks Jack for seeing his band
jokes.punchline: Jack's muted complaint — four hours of blues rock as sacrifice — delivered as dry understatement
jokes.explanation: Functional callback to the Rhythm and News setup. The four-hour detail is a nice escalation but the joke is mostly carried by context. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Liz tells the writers not to write a sketch about Krang from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles — 'No one knows who Krang is. It would be a waste of time to talk about Krang on television. No more Krang!'
jokes.setup: Liz gives writer's room instructions about the walk-on contest sketch
jokes.punchline: She mentions Krang four times while insisting no one knows who Krang is — a meta-joke about the show itself wasting time on an obscure reference
jokes.explanation: A perfect meta-joke: by naming Krang four times while insisting no one knows Krang, the show IS doing exactly what Liz says not to do. It's self-aware, it's about the craft of TV writing, and the escalating repetition ('No more Krang!') is its own comedic structure. 30 Rock at its most self-referential and clever. The joke is also for TMNT fans in the audience who immediately recognize Krang — rewarding the viewer.

jokes.text: Hazel bursts through the door yelling 'Krang!' immediately after Liz's Krang rant
jokes.setup: Liz just finished her 'no more Krang' speech
jokes.punchline: Hazel enters immediately shouting 'Krang!' — presumably having dressed as Krang or referencing a sketch idea — the ultimate ironic punctuation
jokes.explanation: The immediate callback — Hazel entering and shouting 'Krang' literally one second after Liz's speech — is structurally perfect. Economy is a 10: one word is the entire punchline. The joke pays off the preceding meta-joke and simultaneously proves Liz wrong (or right?). A masterclass in comic timing and callback structure.

jokes.text: Liz takes a 'Which Gossip Girl are you?' quiz and gets 'the dad's guitar'
jokes.setup: Hazel asks for Liz's advice 'woman to woman'; Liz questions whether that's a good idea
jokes.punchline: Self-deprecating: she took a personality quiz and was identified as an inanimate object from a teen show — 'the dad's guitar'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant specificity: not 'you got a bad result' but 'the dad's guitar' — a supporting prop from a background character. The joke captures Liz's irrelevance and uncoolness perfectly through an absurd but hyper-specific detail. High quotability because it sounds like something you'd actually say to a friend.

jokes.text: Hazel: 'And look at your body. Your rack is like, "pow!"'
jokes.setup: Hazel flatters Liz while asking for mentorship, calling her an 'Amazon warrior queen'
jokes.punchline: The flattery escalates to Hazel complimenting Liz's breasts directly — a comically inappropriate overstep in a professional mentorship pitch
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe comedy — Hazel's manipulative flattery going too far is character-specific and lands as uncomfortable. Not exceptional but functional.

jokes.text: Kenneth 'undressed her with his eyes' — then: 'And then he had his way with me. With his eyes.'
jokes.setup: Hazel says Kenneth 'undressed her with his eyes' and 'had his way with her'
jokes.punchline: She clarifies 'with his eyes' — the dark implication is walked back, but too late; the audience has already processed the misdirection
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection with a two-beat structure. The pause between 'had his way with me' and 'with his eyes' is the joke. The structure requires good comic timing. The Hazel character's melodrama makes the walk-back funnier.

jokes.text: Liz: 'The male gaze.' Hazel: 'Yeah, they're all a bunch of gays.'
jokes.setup: Liz uses the feminist academic term 'the male gaze'
jokes.punchline: Hazel mishears/misunderstands 'gaze' as 'gays' — a malapropism that reveals her intellectual limitations
jokes.explanation: Efficient joke: 'gaze/gays' is a clean homophone swap that both mocks Hazel's intellect and satirizes feminist jargon in one beat. Liz's correction ('no, Kenneth is sweet, but he's still a man') doesn't fix Hazel's misunderstanding, which adds a layer. High economy.

jokes.text: 'What do people call women who are tough and ambitious?' / 'Leslie or Courtney?' / 'What? No. A bitch.'
jokes.setup: Liz sets up a rhetorical question about society's labels for ambitious women
jokes.punchline: Hazel takes it literally — offering 'Leslie or Courtney' as names — before Liz corrects to the intended answer ('a bitch')
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection on a feminist speech setup. Liz's rhetoric is earnest; Hazel's oblivious literal answer ('Leslie or Courtney') is perfectly timed to undercut the dramatic moment. The specificity of 'Leslie or Courtney' (not just 'a name') makes it funnier — those are actual real-world names for tough women. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Liz invokes 'the karate kid — Hilary Swank-arate Kid IV'
jokes.setup: Liz is giving Hazel an inspirational speech about playing it like a man
jokes.punchline: 'Hilary Swank-arate Kid IV' — a mash-up of Hilary Swank's name and Karate Kid, treating a non-existent film as real reference
jokes.explanation: Clever portmanteau joke ('Swank-arate') with the extra absurdist layer that this film doesn't exist, and Liz cites it as if it does. The joke is in the confidence of the delivery and the specificity of 'IV.' Sets up the fake Mr. Miyagi quote.

jokes.text: Liz does a Mr. Miyagi impression: 'Julie-san, fighting not good. But if must fight, win.' Attributed to 'Kesuke Miyagi, Karate Kid IV.'
jokes.setup: Liz references Karate Kid IV starring Hilary Swank
jokes.punchline: She quotes 'Kesuke Miyagi' from the nonexistent film — using his actual full name, a fake broken-English quote, attributed with citation — and then immediately accepts Hazel's mentorship request
jokes.explanation: The joke builds on #22 — attributing a specific fake quote to a real character from a fictional sequel, with Liz adopting the Miyagi posture before snapping back to accept the mentorship. The 'I accept!' punctuation is perfect. High quotability for 'But if must fight, win.'

jokes.text: Jack calls CNN's Wolf Blitzer: 'Either CNN gets back on the Avery Jessup story, or I'll tell everyone your real name, Steel Hammerhands.'
jokes.setup: Jack tries to get Avery's story covered by calling Wolf Blitzer
jokes.punchline: He threatens to reveal Blitzer's 'real name' — Steel Hammerhands — a ridiculous action-hero name that implies Wolf Blitzer is himself a pseudonym for something even more absurd
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) Wolf Blitzer is itself an absurd-sounding name, so threatening to reveal his 'real name' implies something even more over-the-top; (2) 'Steel Hammerhands' is a perfect action-movie name — specific, ridiculous, and confident; (3) Jack's deadpan delivery of this absurdist blackmail scheme is peak character comedy. The follow-up 'Steel? Mr. Hammerhands?' when no one answers is a great topper. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Jack hangs up, then tries calling back: 'Hello? Steel? Mr. Hammerhands?'
jokes.setup: Jack threatens Blitzer and gets hung up on
jokes.punchline: He calls back using the secret name, treating it with formal address ('Mr. Hammerhands') as if this is a real person's real name
jokes.explanation: The topper to #24 — adding 'Mr. Hammerhands' as a formal address elevates the absurdity. Lean and effective. The joke rewards close attention.

jokes.text: Jenna asks Jack to hire a giant to stand in every scene she's in to make her look daintier — 'It's why Lamar Odom married that giant Kardashian girl.'
jokes.setup: Jenna interrupts Jack's crisis with an 'important actor request'
jokes.punchline: She wants a prop giant for vanity, citing Lamar Odom/Kardashian as proof of concept — a real-world example deployed with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: Pure Jenna character comedy — the vanity request is perfectly in-character and the Kardashian comparison is appropriately absurd. The joke is mostly carried by character recognition.

jokes.text: Jack's fantasy of Avery returning: 'I'm home, Jack. And I brought back a bunch of oriental sex powders.'
jokes.setup: Jack describes sitting in the dark waiting for Avery, then imagines what she'd say
jokes.punchline: His fantasy of a romantic reunion peaks at 'a bunch of oriental sex powders' — a detail revealing Jack's specific, outdated, and slightly absurd vision of marital intimacy
jokes.explanation: The joke is the specificity: not just 'romantic' but 'oriental sex powders' — dated, vaguely imperialist, and completely sincere. Captures Jack's character beautifully. The emotional setup (sitting alone in the dark, waiting) makes the absurd punchline land harder.

jokes.text: 'I played Italian party whore in The Amanda Knox Story.'
jokes.setup: Jenna pitches a TV movie about Avery, citing her experience with the genre
jokes.punchline: Her credential: playing 'Italian party whore' in the Amanda Knox Story — specific, wrong, and perfectly Jenna
jokes.explanation: The role title 'Italian party whore' is perfectly calibrated — specific enough to imply a real credit, absurd enough to be a joke. In four words it captures Jenna's career trajectory and the Lifetime-movie genre being satirized. Very high economy and character integration.

jokes.text: 'Every kidnapped woman I've ever played has been released.'
jokes.setup: Jack is skeptical about trivializing Avery's ordeal with a TV movie
jokes.punchline: Jenna offers her track record as evidence: every kidnapped woman she's played has been released — implying a magical cause-and-effect
jokes.explanation: Jenna treating her on-screen roles as having real-world causal power is perfect character comedy. The line is delivered as a genuine argument, which is the joke. 'Every kidnapped woman I've ever played' also implies a troublingly long list of such roles.

jokes.text: 'Oxygen is already working on a movie about the baby miners.' / 'Then we'll have to slow them down. Gabriel... send a bunch of pies to the Oxygen network.'
jokes.setup: Jenna warns that Oxygen is competing on the baby miners story
jokes.punchline: Jack's executive solution: send pies to Oxygen. A completely absurd corporate sabotage strategy delivered with total authority.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the confidence: Jack doesn't explain why pies will slow down Oxygen, and he doesn't need to. The joke works because it's a recognizably powerful executive cadence ('we'll have to slow them down... Gabriel... send...') applied to an utterly nonsensical order. Also a subtle joke about Oxygen's female audience demographics and associations with food/diet content.

jokes.text: Hazel is making Tracy's food easier to eat because 'his jaw is tired from pretending to be Pac-Man'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks what Hazel is doing; she's preparing Tracy's food in a specific way
jokes.punchline: Tracy's jaw is tired from pretending to be Pac-Man — an absurd but completely plausible Tracy Jordan activity, delivered as a mundane medical accommodation
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy character comedy delivered through implication — we don't see Tracy being Pac-Man, but the idea that he'd do this for long enough to tire his jaw is perfect. 'Pretending to be Pac-Man' is the ideal absurd Tracy Jordan activity. Hazel treating it as routine medical information adds to the comedy.

jokes.text: 'He just got his cholesterol down to triple digits.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth objects to Hazel feeding Tracy junk food
jokes.punchline: Kenneth celebrates Tracy's cholesterol being in 'triple digits' — i.e., still astronomically high (100-999) — as a health victory
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — 'triple digits' sounds like good news until you realize the normal range is under 200, so 'triple digits' as a milestone means Tracy was previously in four digits. The joke rewards a beat of thought and then hits hard. Highly quotable. One of the episode's most efficient jokes.

jokes.text: 'You think you can push me around just because you have a penis?' / Kenneth: 'I definitely have a penis.'
jokes.setup: Hazel accuses Kenneth of sexism
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's earnest, literal, entirely beside-the-point confirmation that he does indeed have a penis
jokes.explanation: Textbook Kenneth Parcell joke: he takes a rhetorical accusation literally and confirms the factual component with complete sincerity. 'I definitely have a penis' is so earnest it circles back to funny. The structure is flawless and the character integration is among the episode's highest. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'I'm not delicate. I've been in tons of car wrecks.'
jokes.setup: Hazel insists she's not a 'delicate little girl'
jokes.punchline: Her proof of toughness: having survived 'tons of car wrecks' — which implies she gets into a lot of car accidents rather than demonstrating strength
jokes.explanation: The logic here is perfect absurdist comedy: car wrecks as evidence of toughness inverts the expected proof while also implying Hazel is perhaps reckless or accident-prone rather than hardy. Clean structure and good character specificity for Hazel's trailer-park background.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Hazel, I just peed this. Could you take care of it for me?' — holding up something (implied urine-adjacent object) mid-argument
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Hazel are arguing over who should care for Tracy
jokes.punchline: Tracy interrupts their power struggle with a completely mundane, degrading request — he just urinated in/on something and needs it handled
jokes.explanation: Tracy's oblivious id-driven behavior cutting through a serious argument is classic. The joke is that the argument about who should care for him is immediately illustrated by how much care he requires. Functional and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Kenneth launches a 'getting-your-act-together montage' song for Tracy — immediately interrupted by Hazel with a piñata
jokes.setup: Kenneth tells Tracy he's in 'dire need of a getting-your-act-together montage' and begins singing
jokes.punchline: Hazel interrupts by offering Tracy a piñata — the montage never happens because Tracy immediately chooses fun over self-improvement
jokes.explanation: Meta in that Kenneth announces the trope ('getting-your-act-together montage') before it begins — and then it's immediately subverted. Tracy's 'Awesome!' at the piñata is the perfect punctuation. The joke also works as character comedy: of course Tracy picks piñata.

jokes.text: Hazel offers Tracy: 'Do you wanna do whatever you want with a sexy, fun bitch who just bought you a piñata?' Tracy: 'Awesome!'
jokes.setup: Hazel competes with Kenneth's montage pitch
jokes.punchline: Her pitch is 'sexy fun bitch with a piñata' — and Tracy's one-word response 'Awesome!' perfectly encapsulates his decision-making process
jokes.explanation: Strong Tracy character moment. The juxtaposition with Kenneth's earnest montage makes this land harder. 'Awesome!' as Tracy's entire cognitive process is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Are you busy regretting your life choices, for example, missing your window for having children?'
jokes.setup: Kenneth approaches Liz to talk about Hazel
jokes.punchline: He asks if she has a second, but immediately offers a specific devastating guess at what she might be doing — regretting her fertility window
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock self-deprecating Liz Lemon joke — even Kenneth, the sweetest character, casually delivers a gut-punch about her biological clock. The specificity of 'missing your window for having children' is perfectly cruel and well-timed.

jokes.text: 'I bet even Hillary Clinton has to put up with this crap from whoever was Secretary of State before her.' / 'You mean Condoleezza—' / 'Shut up.'
jokes.setup: Liz rants about Kenneth not accepting a woman doing his job — invoking Hillary Clinton as an example of female achievement
jokes.punchline: She doesn't know who was Secretary of State before Clinton; Kenneth starts to answer ('Condoleezza—'); Liz preemptively shuts him down
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp joke about feminist rhetoric colliding with ignorance: Liz uses Hillary as a symbol of women overcoming male gatekeeping — without knowing that the predecessor was also a woman (Condoleezza Rice). Kenneth's half-answer and Liz's instant 'shut up' is perfectly structured. The joke is on Liz, but it's also a smart cultural observation. High on all dimensions.

jokes.text: Liz quotes Mr. Miyagi at Kenneth: 'Leave girl alone or you deal with me, surf shop owner.'
jokes.setup: Liz defends Hazel using the Karate Kid framework established earlier
jokes.punchline: The fake Miyagi quote ends with 'surf shop owner' as the threat — an absurdly mundane antagonist in a martial arts context
jokes.explanation: Strong callback that extends the Miyagi running gag. 'Surf shop owner' as the villain of the threat is the joke's core — it's so small and specific as a threat that it works. Extends the fake Karate Kid IV mythology.

jokes.text: Liz's bedroom advice: 'Put a bag of popcorn in the microwave beforehand. That way, when you're done, you have a treat.'
jokes.setup: Hazel calls Liz a 'modern, DTF type woman' with sexual confidence; Liz says she has 'a little bedroom tip'
jokes.punchline: The tip is to microwave popcorn for a post-sex snack — Liz's sexuality filtered entirely through food logistics
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup leads you to expect actual sex advice; the reveal is maximally Liz Lemon — romance reduced to snack optimization. The logic is internally consistent ('that way, when you're done, you have a treat') which makes it funnier. Extremely high quotability and character integration. This is essentially the thesis statement of the Liz Lemon character compressed into two sentences.

jokes.text: Hazel's boyfriend Razmig was 'banging the fattest chick I've ever seen. And you know, I used to weigh 800 pounds.'
jokes.setup: Hazel reveals she caught her boyfriend cheating
jokes.punchline: The qualifier — 'and you know, I used to weigh 800 pounds' — establishes the comparative scale as extreme, making the insult to Hazel specifically devastating
jokes.explanation: The escalation is sharp: 'fattest chick I've ever seen' is already a line, but 'I used to weigh 800 pounds' as context-setter means the woman was truly enormous — and that's the specific insult. Dark and efficient, with a built-in absurdist backstory detail for Hazel.

jokes.text: Hazel's alternative 'mentorship': 'Helping me would be teaching me how to spice things up. Like by greeting him at the front door wearing nothing but false teeth.'
jokes.setup: Hazel rejects Liz's advice to dump Razmig
jokes.punchline: Her alternative solution: greet her cheating boyfriend wearing only false teeth — a non-sequitur sex tip that raises more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist detail. 'Nothing but false teeth' is specific enough to suggest this is from personal experience, wrong enough to be hilarious, and the image it creates is both funny and disturbing. It's quintessentially Hazel — combining sexual confidence with trailer-park specificity. Very high originality and character integration.

jokes.text: 'If this were two years ago, I would sit on you till you died.'
jokes.setup: Hazel expresses disappointment in Liz's mentorship
jokes.punchline: Her expression of frustration is that she used to be large enough to kill someone by sitting on them — implying she weighed enough to fatally crush a person
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback to the 800-pound detail. The threat is so specific and dark that it's genuinely shocking, but the 'two years ago' framing (she's lost the weight, so it's no longer possible) makes it absurdist rather than truly menacing. One of the episode's most quotable lines. The delivery must be deadpan for maximum impact.

jokes.text: Wardrobe scene: Jack dresses up as Gabriel the PA — 'No wigs. I said no wigs. You're not a lead, Gabe. At best, you're a featured extra with no lines.'
jokes.setup: Jack is apparently preparing to go incognito as a background PA named 'Gabe'
jokes.punchline: He's coaching himself/someone about the character's limitations — 'at best a featured extra with no lines' — with all the intensity of a serious actor preparing for a role
jokes.explanation: Context-dependent — funnier in context as we watch Jack prepare to go undercover as a PA. The 'no wigs' instruction implies he initially tried a wig, which is funnier visually. 'Featured extra with no lines' is a very specific actor-ranking joke.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You mean Lois Lane's love affair with journalism?' — responding to Jack asking if she'd write 'the greatest love story ever told'
jokes.setup: Jack asks if Liz wants to write the greatest love story ever told
jokes.punchline: She assumes he means Lois Lane's love of journalism (not a person) — revealing Liz's character priorities: her attachment to fictional characters and media over real romance
jokes.explanation: Sharp character joke: Liz's first instinct for 'greatest love story' is a fictional journalist's relationship with her career. It's both a character-defining moment and a setup-subversion on what 'love story' means. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'I would consider it a personal favor after six years of listening to you complain about how there are so few women on death row.' / 'Is it a coincidence, or is the system sexist?'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz to write the Avery TV movie script by Monday as a personal favor
jokes.punchline: The 'favor' he's owed is for enduring Liz's complaint that there aren't enough women on death row — and Liz immediately re-engages with this cause
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The specificity is extraordinary: Liz's feminist complaint is about the gender gap on death row — a legitimately dark, counterintuitive form of equality advocacy. The two-part structure is perfect: Jack reveals the complaint, and then Liz IMMEDIATELY resumes it ('Is it a coincidence, or is the system sexist?'), confirming she's been complaining about this for years. This is exactly the kind of joke 30 Rock is famous for — absurdist character comedy with real satirical bite. Exceptional on all dimensions.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Oh! Speaking of our amazing dynamic, I have taken on a mentee of my own, Jack — a page named Hazel.' Jack: 'You're a mentor? But that makes me a grand-mentor. And I'm still so young.'
jokes.setup: Liz reveals she's mentoring Hazel
jokes.punchline: Jack's reaction is not about Liz or Hazel — it's about his own vanity ('that makes me a grand-mentor, and I'm still so young')
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack narcissism — his concern is his own age/vitality, not the situation at hand. 'I'm still so young' as a lament about grandparenthood-at-a-remove is very Jack. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: Jack reveals he let Liz fail at the Apollo: 'Sometimes, they have to learn the hard way. If Hazel rejects your advice, let her. She'll get there on her own just like you did after the crowd at the Apollo chased you into the river.'
jokes.setup: Jack advises Liz to let Hazel fail — and then reveals he's done this to Liz
jokes.punchline: The specific failure he let her experience: being chased by an Apollo crowd into a river
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structure: the revelation that Jack has been deliberately letting Liz fail as a mentorship strategy is a genuine surprise, and the specific example ('chased into the river') is hyper-specific and darkly funny. The structure — general advice → implication → specific historical example — is perfectly executed. Liz's dawning realization is the emotional component that makes the joke land harder.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Okay, I understand the irony of what I'm about to say, but I reject that advice. Don't worry, I'll bring you back a t-shirt from successtown. Ow! My groin!'
jokes.setup: Liz confidently rejects Jack's advice about letting people fail, then walks away triumphantly
jokes.punchline: She immediately injures her groin — physical comedy punctuating her bravado
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke: 'successtown' is a nice Liz Lemon coinage for overconfident optimism, and the groin injury is a classic physical comedy punctuation device. The meta-acknowledgment ('I understand the irony') is clever. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'You were wrong. They do still make crossbows.' — Tracy arrives with crossbow and motorcycle ramp but no motorcycle
jokes.setup: Kenneth presumably told Tracy crossbows aren't made anymore; Hazel let him buy one
jokes.punchline: Tracy arrives having purchased a crossbow as vindication, plus a 'motorcycle ramp and no motorcycle' — the ramp without a motorcycle being its own absurdist joke
jokes.explanation: The crossbow-as-argument-winner is funny, but 'a motorcycle ramp and no motorcycle' is the stronger joke — it implies Hazel allowed the most dangerous part of a dangerous activity while omitting the key component. Classic Tracy Jordan consequence logic.

jokes.text: Tracy (off his medication): 'We on a show within a show! My real name is Tracy Morgan!'
jokes.setup: Tracy hasn't slept (needs 14 hours a night or 'goes crazy'); Hazel has taken him off his medication
jokes.punchline: Without meds, Tracy breaks the fourth wall and claims to be actor Tracy Morgan — a meta-joke about the actor/character distinction
jokes.explanation: Perfect meta-comedy: the 'crazy' version of Tracy Jordan is someone who knows he's Tracy Morgan playing a character. The joke works because it's simultaneously true (Tracy Morgan IS playing Tracy Jordan) and absurdist (this is what insanity looks like on this show). High character integration because it's uniquely possible only with this character/actor.

jokes.text: Hazel took Tracy off his medication — 'I'm not an idiot, Kenneth. I took him off his medication.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if Hazel let Tracy drink alcohol (which would be dangerous with his medication)
jokes.punchline: Hazel's answer proves she IS an idiot — she avoided the alcohol/medication combo by eliminating the medication
jokes.explanation: Classic comedy structure: the character protests she's not an idiot, then immediately proves she is. The solution (remove medication to allow drinking) demonstrates a catastrophically backwards logic delivered with complete confidence. Structure is excellent — the 'not an idiot' setup makes the punchline sharper.

jokes.text: Hazel shows Kenneth a Page Six photo: 'Those are my toes he's sucking on. And he did not want to.'
jokes.setup: Hazel justifies exploiting Tracy for fame — she's gotten into Page Six
jokes.punchline: 'And he did not want to' — confirming this was coerced toe-sucking from a celebrity, presented as a PR win
jokes.explanation: Extremely dark and specific. 'And he did not want to' is devastating — it acknowledges the coercion matter-of-factly as just part of the hustle. The Hazel character's complete moral obliviousness is the joke. Very high economy ('And he did not want to' is five words doing enormous comedic work).

jokes.text: Jenna tries to play Avery by sneaking into Jack's office pretending to be her — 'No, don't turn on the light.'
jokes.setup: Jack's phone rings — a UN contact says Avery has been found and dropped off at his office
jokes.punchline: It's Jenna pretending to be Avery in order to audition for the role — 'Don't turn on the light' suggests she's relying on darkness for the illusion
jokes.explanation: The joke is structured as a genuine emotional payoff (Avery returns!) immediately revealed as Jenna's scheme. The audacity of the plan — using the UN as a fake call, sneaking into his dark office — is perfectly Jenna. The darkness detail implies the illusion would fail in light, which is its own joke.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'You think I'm stupid, just because my college got tipped over by those Miami Heat fans.'
jokes.setup: Jack implies Jenna isn't educated enough to play Avery, who went to Yale.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's college was physically 'tipped over' by basketball fans — an absurd image that sidesteps the question of whether she actually graduated.
jokes.explanation: College getting 'tipped over' is a perfectly absurd and specific image. It implies the school was so precarious it could be toppled, and Jenna treats it as a normal thing that happens. The Miami Heat specificity adds texture. Justifies 8.3.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Jenna, there are many kinds of intelligence. Practical, emotional, and there's actual intelligence, which is what I'm talking about.'
jokes.setup: Jack tries to soften the blow of calling Jenna stupid.
jokes.punchline: His diplomatic list of intelligences ends with 'actual intelligence' as the third and distinct category — implying the first two don't count.
jokes.explanation: Jack's diplomatic taxonomy of intelligence that ends by nullifying the first two is a sharp construction. 'Actual intelligence' as the third type is both the insult and the punchline. Tight structure, strong Jack characterization.

jokes.text: 'Let's set aside how idiotic that plan was and imagine a world where it actually worked.'
jokes.setup: Jenna's fake-Avery plan is exposed
jokes.punchline: Jack's response is to engage with the hypothetical of the plan working rather than address its insanity — treating it as a thought experiment
jokes.explanation: Jack's response is beautifully composed — rather than anger, he does rhetorical judo, acknowledging idiocy and then engaging anyway. 'Imagine a world where it actually worked' is both sophisticated and funny in its detachment. Solid character beat.

jokes.text: 'Would a dumb person be able to think of something amazing to say as she leaves?' — Jenna then stands there for ten seconds in silence, unable to think of anything
jokes.setup: Jenna challenges Jack's implication that she's stupid by asking if a dumb person could think of an amazing exit line
jokes.punchline: Long pause — she cannot think of anything — and then she leaves without saying it, proving his point
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-structured jokes. The setup is a classic 'watch me do something impressive' challenge; the punchline is the absence of anything — silence proves the opposite of what Jenna claimed. The joke requires the actor to commit to the pause (estimated ~10-12 seconds), which is extremely difficult to pull off on television. Economy is perfect: no words in the punchline. The structure is almost mathematically elegant. Tied for episode high.

jokes.text: Contest winner is 'Joren van der Sloot' — 'We can't fly someone from Peru now.'
jokes.setup: Liz randomly picks a contest essay
jokes.punchline: The winner is Joran van der Sloot — the Dutch man convicted of murder in Peru, referencing the Natalee Holloway case — who would need to be flown from a Peruvian prison
jokes.explanation: Dark celebrity/news reference joke — Joran van der Sloot entering a walk-on contest while imprisoned in Peru is a darkly absurd premise. The practical objection ('we can't fly someone from Peru') treats the real problem as logistics rather than the obvious issue. Works better for audiences with the cultural reference.

jokes.text: Razmig appears: 'What? Who is this, hah-zel? I no permit you talk other woman.' — caricatured Armenian accent and possessive control framed comedically
jokes.setup: Hazel's terrible boyfriend Razmig shows up in the room
jokes.punchline: He immediately forbids Hazel from talking to other women — a controlling red flag delivered in broad caricature accent
jokes.explanation: The weakest recurring joke in the episode. The accent caricature is broad and lazy — relying on stereotype rather than wit. The abuser-as-comedy-character framing is uncomfortable without being clever. The joke exists to make Hazel's poor choices legible but the execution is reductive.

jokes.text: Razmig: 'Oh, where is toilet pail? Razmig must make mud.' — Hazel laughs
jokes.setup: Liz argues Razmig is no good; Hazel insists 'he makes me laugh'
jokes.punchline: The thing that makes her laugh is Razmig asking for a 'toilet pail' to 'make mud' — his description of using the bathroom
jokes.explanation: Again relies heavily on accent caricature and bathroom humor. 'Make mud' as a euphemism is mildly amusing but the joke is mostly carried by the visual contrast between Hazel's laughter and Liz's mortification. Weak by 30 Rock standards.

jokes.text: Razmig: 'You are a big woman. You have pictures? Fat nudes?'
jokes.setup: Hazel tells Liz 'it takes a big woman to admit she's wrong'
jokes.punchline: Razmig takes 'big woman' literally and asks Liz for fat nude photos — referencing Hazel's former 800-pound weight
jokes.explanation: Better than the other Razmig jokes because it connects to established character detail (Hazel's former weight) and has an actual setup/punchline structure. Still relies on the lazy caricature accent, but the callback to the 800-pound detail adds a layer.

jokes.text: Jenna to Kenneth: 'Oh, I thought you were someone famous. You sound a lot like Reese Witherspoon.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth knocks on Jenna's door and asks for help
jokes.punchline: Jenna's disappointment that he's not famous, combined with the bizarre claim that he sounds like Reese Witherspoon
jokes.explanation: Classic Jenna character joke: her threshold for caring about someone is fame. The Reese Witherspoon comparison is random enough to be funny — there's no obvious reason Kenneth would sound like Reese Witherspoon, and Jenna doesn't explain it.

jokes.text: Kenneth quits his job at Standards and Practices to enter the walk-on contest — the Standards and Practices employee responds: 'I may f***ing hate you right now, you little f***, but f***ing damn it I respect you.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains he quit his NBC job to enter a contest as a civilian
jokes.punchline: The Standards and Practices employee (Gaylord Felcher) responds with a string of bleeps expressing grudging respect — the censorship department censoring itself again
jokes.explanation: Strong callback to the Standards and Practices joke — the department continues to bleep itself in ironic self-censorship. The emotional content ('I may f***ing hate you but I respect you') is also a genuine character moment played for laughs. The bleep-heavy profanity is funnier in context because the audience now knows this is how this department operates.

jokes.text: Kenneth, in a disguise/costume as a contest winner, enters as 'Leminem' — a portmanteau of Liz Lemon and Eminem.
jokes.setup: Jenna tells Kenneth to 'play the part' to get around Hazel and reach Tracy.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's chosen disguise is 'Leminem' — a costume implying he dressed as a cross between Liz Lemon and Eminem. The name is announced at the show's closing.
jokes.explanation: 'Leminem' is a great portmanteau name. The visual of Kenneth in that costume (implied) is funnier in imagination. The name also works as a joke on its own — Lemon + Eminem, two unlikely combos.

jokes.text: Kenneth quits his Standards and Practices job to enter the walk-on contest. The Standards employee's send-off: 'I may [bleep] hate you right now, you little [bleep], but [bleep] damn it I respect you.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains he quit his job to qualify as a non-NBC employee for the contest.
jokes.punchline: The foul-mouthed Standards department send-off is a callback to the earlier award ceremony bleeping — the department is consistently profane, and the send-off is both heartfelt and profane.
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the running gag of the Standards department being ironically profane. The heartfelt-but-bleeped farewell is a clean execution of the bit.

jokes.text: Kenneth explains his motivation for quitting: 'Have you ever loved something so much that you would sacrifice anything for it?' Liz: 'Nope.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth makes an earnest speech about unconditional love and sacrifice
jokes.punchline: Liz's flat, immediate 'Nope' — she has not experienced this feeling
jokes.explanation: A one-word punchline that does enormous character work: Kenneth's earnestness is maximum, Liz's response is minimum. 'Nope' is the funniest possible answer and completely character-consistent — Liz doesn't have that kind of emotional depth, or admits she doesn't. Economy score nearly perfect.

jokes.text: 'The second cruelest thing anyone has ever done to me.' / 'When I went to the bathroom on the hood of your car before I thought of this plan?'
jokes.setup: Jack calls Jenna a monster and says what she did is 'the second cruelest thing'
jokes.punchline: Jenna correctly identifies the first: she urinated on Jack's car hood before deciding to impersonate his wife
jokes.explanation: The structure is exceptional: 'second cruelest thing' creates an expectation, and Jenna's guess — she peed on his car *before* the plan, so it's a separate offense — recontextualizes her entire scheme. The detail that she went to the bathroom on his car hood AS an earlier act implies a pattern of abuse. Very high character integration for Jenna.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Avery had me committed to a mental hospital so she and her college roommate could use my Yankee tickets on opening day.'
jokes.setup: Jenna asks what the cruelest thing done to Jack was
jokes.punchline: Avery had him institutionalized — not for love or care — but to steal his baseball tickets
jokes.explanation: Superb character joke — it reveals that Avery's 'ruthless pursuit of self-interest' (praised later in the episode) extends to having her husband committed for Yankees tickets. The specificity ('opening day,' 'her college roommate') makes the betrayal comedically rich. This also functions as setup for the conclusion where Jack celebrates Avery's ruthlessness as her defining quality.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'That's a nice story, Jack, but I don't hear my name in it.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Jenna the story of Avery committing him for Yankee tickets
jokes.punchline: Jenna's response is pure narcissism — she dismisses the poignant story because it doesn't involve her
jokes.explanation: A maximally efficient character joke: nine words that perfectly capture Jenna's entire personality. 'I don't hear my name in it' as the criterion for whether a story matters is a perfect distillation of her narcissism. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jack concludes Jenna has 'Avery's essence' — 'the ruthless pursuit of self-interest. It's the heart of capitalism. And the beautiful black heart of my wife.' — then congratulates Jenna and she accepts 'the part.'
jokes.setup: Jack has been saying Jenna doesn't have Avery's 'essence'; Jenna has just demonstrated total self-interest
jokes.punchline: Jack reframes Jenna's awfulness as proof she's perfect for the role — the 'essence' being sociopathic self-interest
jokes.explanation: Strong concluding joke for the A-plot: Jack's celebration of 'ruthless pursuit of self-interest' as a virtue is perfectly in character, and it ties together Jenna's behavior with Avery's established character. 'Beautiful black heart of my wife' is an excellent line.

jokes.text: 'Now if you'll excuse me, I have a female condom to take out. Unless... Going once...'
jokes.setup: Jenna gets the part and thanks Jack
jokes.punchline: She offers to take out a female condom — implying she came prepared for the possibility of a casting-couch scenario — and tests if Jack is interested before leaving
jokes.explanation: Dark and very Jenna — she had a female condom prepped as a possible negotiating tool. 'Going once' as a casual auction-style offer is a great comedic framing. Jack's 'Four, three—' countdown response (telling the crew to count down to air) works as both a rejection and a callback to the show happening in real time.

jokes.text: Tracy's presidential address: 'Goo-goo, ga-ga, my fellow ah-meh-ri-cans.'
jokes.setup: A presidential address begins during the live TGS broadcast.
jokes.punchline: Tracy, unmedicated and sleep-deprived, begins the address in baby talk with a phonetic exaggeration of 'Americans.'
jokes.explanation: Tracy's degraded state manifesting as a presidential address in baby talk is a great convergence of the episode's plot threads. 'Ah-meh-ri-cans' is a funny phonetic choice. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Kenneth to Tracy: 'I won't do that' (quoting Meat Loaf's 'I'd Do Anything for Love') — Tracy: 'The girl in that video was hot in an early '90s kind of way.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth makes an emotional speech about doing anything for love but refusing to stand by while Tracy destroys himself
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response to Kenneth's emotional declaration is to review the attractiveness of the Meat Loaf music video actress
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy — Kenneth's sincere Meat Loaf reference goes completely over Tracy's head, who processes it purely as a music video memory. 'Hot in an early '90s kind of way' is a perfectly Tracy observation: oddly specific, period-accurate, and completely beside the point. The joke is the chasm between Kenneth's emotional sincerity and Tracy's response.

jokes.text: 'That was a real commercial for an erectile dysfunction drug.' / Jack: 'Well, I laughed.'
jokes.setup: Jack says the sketch about a man worried about sexual performance was 'all right'; Liz points out it was an actual ED commercial
jokes.punchline: Jack's response: 'Well, I laughed.' — treating a pharmaceutical ad as indistinguishable from the comedy show
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-joke about television quality — Jack can't tell the difference between the comedy show and an ED commercial, implying TGS is so bad that pharmaceutical ads are comparable. The three-word punchline 'Well, I laughed' is near-perfect economy. This also works as an NBC/network TV self-deprecation joke, which is classic 30 Rock.

jokes.text: 'That's how the banking industry learned its lesson. And now they're doing amazing, and everyone's honest.'
jokes.setup: Jack defends his 'let them fail' mentoring philosophy as something that works — citing the banking industry
jokes.punchline: The banking industry is cited as a success story of learning through failure — a bitterly ironic reference to the 2008 financial crisis and its aftermath
jokes.explanation: Sharp political comedy. Jack's sincere endorsement of the banking industry post-crisis as 'doing amazing, and everyone's honest' is perfectly calibrated irony — he genuinely believes this. The joke is both character-specific (Jack as Wall Street apologist) and topical satire. 'Everyone's honest' is the perfect escalating absurdist closer. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Why aren't there more female serial killers? What does that say about our society—' Jack: 'Liz!'
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz's post-show debrief appears to be winding down
jokes.punchline: Liz pivots to a new complaint — the gender gap among serial killers — as a feminist issue, mid-conversation, requiring Jack to interrupt her
jokes.explanation: A callback and escalation of joke #47 — Liz's death row gender gap concern has expanded to serial killers. This confirms it's a running feminist critique that's evolved during their conversation. Jack's interruption ('Liz!') is perfect — he's already had to shut this down once today. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Hazel's garbled summary of Liz's mentorship advice: 'Hazel, you're a beautiful flower. Let yourself bloom. What are you doing this weekend, Hazel? Are there still bath houses? Let's go to one!'
jokes.setup: Hazel says she finally heard Liz's voice and understood her guidance
jokes.punchline: The 'guidance' she heard is a completely fabricated series of statements Liz never said — including inviting Hazel to a bathhouse
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates from plausibly paraphrased ('you're a beautiful flower') to increasingly bizarre fabrications ('are there still bath houses? Let's go to one!'). The structure tracks the escalation perfectly. Liz's 'I never said any of that, but—' is the perfect response — she can't fully deny the good outcome even if the quotes are wrong.

jokes.text: 'And all the while lighting a fire with that hot ass.' — Hazel to Liz
jokes.setup: Hazel's sincere expression of gratitude to Liz for her mentorship
jokes.punchline: She concludes her heartfelt speech by complimenting Liz's buttocks — an inappropriate pivot from professional gratitude to physical admiration
jokes.explanation: Hazel's inappropriate boundary violations are a running character trait. The placement (at the end of an earnest thank-you speech) is well-timed. Functional cringe comedy but not the episode's sharpest.

jokes.text: Jack looks at Liz warmly after Hazel leaves: 'I'm your grand-mentor. Liz?' — she's gone. He looks at the empty space: 'She's beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Jack has an emotional realization about his mentorship chain
jokes.punchline: He turns to share the moment with Liz, but she's left; he addresses the empty space, calling her 'beautiful' — a moment of genuine (absurd) pride
jokes.explanation: A quiet, well-executed character beat: Jack's genuine pride in his 'grand-mentorship' is undercut by Liz having left without ceremony. 'She's beautiful' addressed to empty air is both a joke and a genuine character moment. The episode's emotional button, executed with the right blend of sincerity and absurdity.

jokes.text: End tag: 'Please welcome to the stage: Leminem!' — scattered applause and booing, then Tracy begins poorly doing the sprinkler dance while rapping badly
jokes.setup: A TGS segment introduces what appears to be a musical guest
jokes.punchline: 'Leminem' — a portmanteau of Liz Lemon and Eminem — performed by Tracy, with bad rapping and the sprinkler dance to scattered applause and boos
jokes.explanation: A satisfying cold-close joke: 'Leminem' as a portmanteau is clever, and Tracy performing it badly with the sprinkler is visual comedy that works both on screen and as character comedy (of course Tracy created this). The 'scattered applause, booing' reaction is perfect in context.

tmdb_overview: Liz struggles in her new role as mentor to Hazel. Kenneth has a difficult time letting go of his page duties and takes drastic measures to make sure Tracy is taken care of. Meanwhile, Jack and Jenna come up with a plan to get Avery back in the headlines.
insight: 67 jokes in 26 minutes: 30 Rock hits elite density with character-driven absurdism.
